blocks.text: Almost every binary tree solution has the same shape. Once you see it, most tree problems become a matter of filling in two blanks: **what does an empty tree return**, and **how do I combine my children's answers with my own value**.

blocks.code:
solve(node):
    if node is null:   return the answer for an empty tree     <- base case
    left  = solve(node.left)                                   <- trust it
    right = solve(node.right)                                  <- trust it
    return combine(node.val, left, right)

blocks.text: The hard part is the middle two lines: you have to **trust** that the recursive calls return the right answer for the subtrees, without tracing them in your head. That isn't magic — it's induction. If `solve` is right for smaller trees (and it's right for the empty tree), then combining their answers correctly makes it right for this tree too.

blocks.alt: Summing the tree 5, 3, 8, 1, 4. Each leaf returns its own value: 1, 4 and 8. Node 3 combines 3 + 1 + 4 = 8. The root combines 5 + 8 + 8 = 21. Answers flow up the tree.

blocks.caption: Watch the call stack grow on the way down and the answers come back up.

blocks.text: Swap the blanks and the same code computes almost anything: **size** (`1 + left + right`), **height** (`1 + max(left, right)`), **maximum value** (`max(val, left, right)`), **number of leaves** (`left + right`, or 1 at a leaf).
Two directions: answers up, information down
Information can travel through the recursion in two directions, and most problems use one of them — some use both:

items: **Bottom-up (return values)** — each call **returns** something about its subtree, and the parent combines. Sum, height, size, "is it balanced", lowest common ancestor.

**Top-down (parameters)** — each call **receives** something about the path above it, and passes an updated version to its children. Depth so far, the running sum from the root, the path so far, the largest value seen on the way down.

blocks.text: A classic top-down example: count the **good** nodes — those where no node on the path from the root down to them has a bigger value. Each call only needs to know the **largest value seen so far**, so pass it down:

blocks.alt: Counting good nodes in the tree 3, 1, 4, 3, null, 1, 5. The maximum seen so far is passed down: root 3 (max 3, good), 1 (max 3, not good), 4 (max 4, good), 3 under 1 (max 3, good), 1 under 4 (max 4, not good), 5 (max 5, good). Four good nodes.

blocks.text: Notice that this one uses **both** directions: the maximum travels **down** as a parameter, and the count of good nodes travels **up** as the return value.

Recursion is a stack you don't see — the **call stack**. You can always replace it with an explicit stack of nodes still to visit. This avoids running out of call stack on a very deep (skewed) tree, at the cost of slightly longer code:

blocks.alt: Memory used by recursion equals the tree's height. A balanced tree of 7 nodes needs at most 3 frames on the call stack. A skewed chain of 7 nodes needs 7.

elements.text:
time:  O(n) - every node is visited once
space: O(h) - one call frame per level of the current path
       h is about log n when balanced, n for a chain

items: **Forgetting the null case** — `node.left.val` crashes when there is no left child. Let the base case handle null, and don't look at a child's value before checking it exists.
**Mixing up depth and height** — depth counts down from the root; height counts up from the leaves.
**Treating a null child as a leaf** — a leaf is a node whose **both** children are null. A node with one child is not a leaf, even though one of its calls hits null.
**Sharing a list without undoing changes** — if you pass one path list down and append to it, remove the value again on the way back up (**backtracking**), or every branch sees the others' values.
**Recomputing the same thing** — calling `height()` inside another recursion at every node costs O(n²). Return more than one value at once instead.
Template: **base case for null**, solve the **left** and **right** subtrees, **combine**.
Answers flow **up** through return values; context flows **down** through parameters.
Recursion is a hidden stack; an explicit **stack** (DFS) or **queue** (BFS) does the same without recursion.
Cost: **O(n) time** and **O(h) space** — between O(log n) and O(n) depending on the shape.
